# Apple Human Interface Guidelines

Use the relevant Apple guidance to make concrete design decisions. This package
contains a router, 13 family routes, 158 operational topic skills, and supporting
article-level references. It is
independent of Apple. The sources are a dated English HIG snapshot; check the
official source when a task depends on a newer release or a disputed detail.

## Route the task

1. Identify the target platform, device context, and user task from the request or
   project. Ask for the platform only when it materially affects the answer and
   cannot be inferred. Preserve the user's framework and product requirements.
2. Select the relevant family below and read that family's `SKILL.md`. Follow its
   link to the exact topic procedure under `.topics/` and read that `SKILL.md`.
   Apply its decision procedure, then consult its supporting article for facts
   and platform qualifications. Topic skills are explicitly read by installed
   file path; automatic nested discovery is not required.
   For platform support, product feasibility, or platform adaptation, first read each relevant
   platform's Getting started procedure, then the specific component or technology
   procedure. Check both the platform model and the surface's support limits.
3. Before finalizing the route, search the [complete topic index](references/topic-index.md)
   for the task's concepts as well as component or framework names. Its trigger
   descriptions connect everyday product requests to Apple's topic names; users
   need not name an Apple framework. Read the owning family and matching topic
   procedure before its supporting reference. Search relevant rows instead of
   loading the full corpus for a narrow question.
   For a screenshot-specific or animated example, also consult its
   [original visual explanation](references/media/index.md) when available.
4. Apply shared guidance and the target platform's documented differences. A
   missing platform subsection means no additional rule is stated; it does not
   prove support, nonapplicability, or identical behavior across platforms.
5. Compose families when the task crosses them: a component can also require
   accessibility, typography, localization, input, or system-experience guidance.
   Map the brief's material decisions to their owning topics. Read the owning
   procedure for each explicit concern, such as privacy or accessibility, as well
   as the affected components; a neighboring procedure's reminder is insufficient.
   Use [platform and task routes](references/platforms-and-tasks.md) when useful.
   In a review, map each supplied control to its candidate component procedure
   even when markup or behavior is missing. Use it to frame inspection questions;
   missing evidence neither proves a defect nor removes that control from scope.

All paths are relative to **this installed package**, not the shell's current
directory. No Python, network, sibling skill installation, or authoring cache is
required to read the guidance.

## Perform the requested work

Inspect the supplied brief, flow, code, specification or image before deciding
what is wrong or choosing a framework. Use the user's requested mode:

- **Design:** produce an implementable specification or interaction/state model
  from the topic's decision procedure, with concrete transitions and acceptance
  checks. Connect choices to the user's task and target platform.
- **Implement:** prefer the project's native system components when they supply
  the needed behavior. HIG explains experience requirements; verify API names,
  availability, and code against the appropriate SDK documentation. Make the
  authorized changes in the existing stack; a prose explanation alone does not
  complete an implementation request.
- **Review:** describe the observed problem, its effect, the relevant HIG rule,
  and a concrete correction. Separate source-backed findings from your own
  suggested improvements. Do not invent violations without inspecting evidence.
- **Adapt:** preserve the product task, data and useful state while applying the
  destination platform's interaction model. Patch the supplied artifact or give
  an explicit before/after contract when a design specification is requested.

Topic procedures are framework agnostic. Their worked examples and pseudocode
teach decisions, not a requirement to replace the project's technology. Load
related procedures only for a decision that actually depends on them.

Complete the topic's observable checks and report passed, failed and not executed
separately. Reading a file, citing Apple, or proposing a test does not establish
runtime behavior. Static code or screenshots cannot prove assistive-technology
order, native rendering, physical comfort, haptics, or SDK compilation.

Include official article/section links for material recommendations. Preserve
qualifications such as “consider,” “prefer,” and “avoid”; do not turn design
advice into invented universal requirements. Retain units and platform scope for
numerical specifications. If source passages conflict, describe the conflict
and the conservative application rather than silently changing the source.

## Source boundaries

This is comprehensive local guidance, not a verbatim Apple manual or an SDK API
reference. Original media explanations are supplementary to article references;
the source page remains useful for visual demonstrations. Source snapshots and
review status live in the repository's coverage report, outside ordinary skill
loading. Do not infer that a source has been independently reviewed just because
its local file exists.

Historical `navigation-bars` links now resolve to current Toolbars guidance;

current rules. Translations, archived pages, and complete linked SDK/WWDC libraries
are outside the source boundary.

description: Use when creating, reviewing, or adapting an iPhone experience for handheld touch, interrupted use, orientation changes, and system entrypoints.

# Make the iPhone task usable in the hand

Read [Designing for iOS](../../references/designing-for-ios.md). Inspect the current task, its entry and return points, supported orientations, input, and any supplied implementation. Distinguish a brief check from extended work. For a review, anchor problems to supplied screens/behavior; for design or adaptation, revise the requested artifact in its existing stack.

Choose what must remain immediately visible during the task. A brief check needs its result and primary action close together; extended editing can expose additional controls without crowding the initial screen. Put frequent touch actions within comfortable reach, generally toward the middle/lower display, while preserving system navigation and swipe-back behavior. Move secondary commands into a short discoverable path rather than shrinking every control to fit.

Trace interruption and resumption: preserve the selected item, draft, or playback context when another app takes focus. Specify portrait/landscape and enlarged-text rearrangements without inventing a new navigation hierarchy for each orientation. Use touch and onscreen keyboard as the baseline, then offer appropriate voice or accessory paths. Add location, biometric, payment, or motion features only when their benefit reduces task effort and access is appropriate.

For repeated out-of-app actions, choose a relevant system entrypoint and a precise destination: a quick action starts an action, search opens the found content, and a widget exposes a useful glance. Do not add every entrypoint to every app.

**Before → decision → after:** A parcel app opens a dense desktop-style table and requires opening three menus to find the latest delivery. A handheld glance needs delivery state first. The revised home screen shows the active parcel and “Show pickup code,” keeps history one step away, and returns a widget tap to that parcel rather than a generic home screen.

Deliver a revised screen/flow or implementation plus interruption, orientation, and text-size acceptance checks. Fail if the primary action becomes unreachable, Back conflicts with a custom gesture, or resuming loses work. Screenshot review cannot establish touch comfort or actual system integration; state pending device checks.

For detailed adaptation use [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md); for custom touch gestures use [Gestures](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-gestures/SKILL.md); for a chosen glance use [Widgets](../../../apple-hig-system-experiences/.topics/apple-hig-widgets/SKILL.md).

name: apple-hig-designing-for-ipados

# Use the iPad canvas without assuming exclusive space

Read [Designing for iPadOS](../../references/designing-for-ipados.md). Inspect the task, related content, current navigation, window assumptions, and supported touch/Pencil/keyboard/pointer paths. Identify whether people hold the iPad or work at a stand/table. Establish design, review, or adaptation mode and revise only the authorized surface using the existing stack.

Decide which relationships benefit from simultaneous visibility. Keep a list beside detail or tools beside a canvas when that reduces navigation; leave unrelated information out. Replace repeated full-screen transitions or modal panels with persistent contextual structure when space permits. At compact multitasking widths, collapse that structure while retaining selection, draft, and the route back to context.

Map each meaningful operation to the inputs the task supports. Touch remains usable without attached accessories. Precise pointer selection and keyboard commands can accelerate work; Pencil may create or annotate content without becoming a required substitute for ordinary controls. Let input methods change during the same task without discarding state or hiding essential commands behind hover.

For cross-app work, specify what can be dragged out/in and where imported content lands. Treat resizing, orientation, larger text, and another app's presence as normal operating conditions. If the iPad experience runs on Mac, identify the Mac adaptation work rather than claiming identical behavior is already native.

**Worked transformation:** Before, a sheet-music editor copies its phone flow: choose score, open full-screen tools, then return to the page after each change. Decision: editing needs score and tools together, but multitasking may narrow the window. After, a contextual tool column accompanies the score at regular width and becomes a dismissible panel at compact width, preserving page, selection, and undo history. Touch editing and keyboard commands reach the same operations.

Deliver a wide/narrow task flow and input mapping or corresponding implementation. Fail if shrinking loses a selected object, a pointer-only control blocks touch, or imported content silently replaces work. Use supplied evidence for findings; physical reach, Pencil response, and inter-app drag/drop remain unverified until exercised on supported devices.

Continue with [Layout](../../../apple-hig-foundations/.topics/apple-hig-layout/SKILL.md) for resizing, [Apple Pencil and Scribble](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-apple-pencil-and-scribble/SKILL.md) for drawing/writing, or [Pointing devices](../../../apple-hig-inputs/.topics/apple-hig-pointing-devices/SKILL.md) for precision input.

# Preserve item identity through layout changes

Read [the collection guide](../../references/collections.md). The workflow is application advice, with documented support qualified by platform.

Inspect actual items, screen/code, target input/platform, and create/review/adapt intent. Determine whether visual recognition or text comparison drives selection; record selection, reorder, insertion, and scrolling behavior only when evidenced. Text-heavy comparison may belong in a list/table rather than a collection.

Choose a familiar row/grid before a custom arrangement. Size cells around meaningful imagery and labels, allowing focus/hover expansion without collision. Retain standard selection/editing interactions and use custom gestures only for a demonstrated task need. For iOS/iPadOS layout changes during manipulation, favor explicit triggers and preserve the person's location and selected item; do not reshuffle a live grid merely because a data property changed. The guide marks collections unsupported on watchOS, so adapt to a suitable list rather than assert parity.

Implement a requested collection or produce a cell/layout/interaction specification; review findings must name affected items or transitions. Specify stable identity and understandable insertion/deletion/reorder feedback as application decisions consistent with the guide.

**Worked transformation:** Before: a wallpaper grid reorders by popularity while someone drags an image, causing the target to move. Decision: dynamic ranking conflicts with manipulation. After: preserve the displayed order during the drag and expose an explicit refresh/sort action; animate a deliberate reorder while retaining selection.

Deliver the artifact and layout-change policy. Verify long labels, odd item counts, focused edge cells, reorder, and deletion of the selected item. Fail for overlapping focused cells, accidental activation during scrolling, or identity/location lost after a layout change. Report native focus/gesture execution separately from inspected logic.

Use [lists-and-tables](../apple-hig-lists-and-tables/SKILL.md) for text comparison, [image-views](../../../apple-hig-content/.topics/apple-hig-image-views/SKILL.md) for fitting, or [drag-and-drop](../../../apple-hig-patterns/.topics/apple-hig-drag-and-drop/SKILL.md) for transfer behavior.

# Make the task accessible

Read [Accessibility guidance](../../references/accessibility.md) before applying platform values. This procedure turns that guidance into task-level changes; its artifact format and prioritization are application engineering advice, not additional Apple requirements.

## Establish what can be evaluated

Identify the supported platform, the person's task from entry to completion, and whether the request is design, review, or adaptation. Inspect the supplied screens, content, interaction description, semantics, or implementation. Record which evidence exists: a screenshot can establish visible labels and geometry, but cannot establish spoken names, focus order, alternative activation, or preference behavior. Continue using explicit assumptions when the platform or behavior is missing; ask only when the choice changes the requested result.

For a review, connect each finding to an observed barrier and its consequence for that task. Separate untested behavior needing verification from confirmed defects. For a design or adaptation, change the authorized artifact itself: a revised screen specification, interaction contract, or implementation. A general accessibility checklist alone is not the deliverable.

## Remove the barriers that the task contains

Trace the task without assuming sight, hearing, fine motor control, speech, or fast responses. Select the applicable branches:

- **Reading and visual distinctions:** Preserve content and available actions when text enlarges. Use the guide's platform-specific text defaults and minima; its resizing guidance is at least 200%, with 140% stated for watchOS. Reflow or expose another usable arrangement rather than clipping essential labels. Pair color distinctions with text, shape, or symbols. Evaluate actual foreground/background combinations in light and dark appearances; use a contrast calculator and preserve the guide's stated contrast-table scope instead of claiming that its values alone establish conformance. If the default scheme falls short, specify the Increase Contrast treatment.
- **Information carried by sound or imagery:** Identify what information would disappear when sound or sight is unavailable. Choose captions for synchronized audible events, subtitles for dialogue translation, audio description for visual events, or transcripts for a complete text account according to the content. Specify descriptions for meaningful interface/content imagery and omit redundant decoration. Pair essential sound feedback with a perceivable visual or appropriate haptic equivalent.
- **Manipulation and navigation:** Distinguish visible control size from its actual activation area and separation. Use the guide's platform default as the starting point; its smaller minimum is not a blanket recommendation for dense controls. Replace essential complex or repeated gestures with a labeled onscreen action. Make the complete task navigable and activatable with the supported keyboard and assistive input paths; speech must not be necessary. Preserve system accessibility shortcuts. For custom controls, specify names, roles, values, states, and task order rather than assuming their appearance supplies semantics.

Reduce spring bounce; tie appropriate motion directly to gestures; avoid animated depth changes and blur transitions; replace spatial translations with fades. Fast or blinking motion can distract, cause dizziness, or trigger seizures. Independent media review is recorded separately in the coverage report. ## Contents - [Ensuring legibility](#Ensuring-legibility) - [Conveying hierarchy](#Conveying-hierarchy) - [Using system fonts](#Using-system-fonts) - [Using custom fonts](#Using-custom-fonts) - [Supporting Dynamic Type](#Supporting-Dynamic-Type) - [Platform considerations](#Platform-considerations) - [Specifications](#Specifications) - [Resources](#Resources) - [Change log](#Change-log) ## Ensuring legibility Test type at real viewing distances, lighting conditions, and supported devices. Enlarge hard-to-read text, improve foreground/background contrast, or choose a more legible face. Prefer Regular, Medium, Semibold, or Bold over Ultralight/Thin/Light, especially at small sizes. Thin custom faces often need sizes above the recommendations. |Platform|Default|Minimum| |---|---:|---:| |iOS, iPadOS|17 pt|11 pt| |macOS|13 pt|10 pt| |tvOS|29 pt|23 pt| |visionOS|17 pt|12 pt| |watchOS|16 pt|12 pt| ## Conveying hierarchy Combine size, weight, and color to distinguish levels, and preserve those relationships as text grows. Limit typeface families so differences retain meaning. Prioritize content people intend to read when scaling: body/dialogue may need growth while tab labels or transient damage numbers need not grow equally. ## Using system fonts San Francisco includes Pro, Compact, Arabic, Armenian, Georgian, Hebrew, and Mono variants; all listed except Mono also have rounded alternatives. New York is a complementary serif family. Variable fonts interpolate weights and optical design continuously for the exact point size, rather than requiring separate Text/Display font choices except in limited design tools. SF offers widths such as Condensed/Expanded and weights from Ultralight through Black; equivalent SF Symbol weights enable precise matching. Use semantic text styles to express hierarchy through coordinated weight, size, and leading, and to inherit Dynamic Type/accessibility adjustments where supported. Modify symbolic traits for emphasis or line spacing when justified. Loose leading supports long passages or wide columns; tight leading can fit constrained rows, but avoid it for three or more lines. Access system fonts through platform APIs (`default`, `serif`, and the font-design constants), without embedding the files. Runtime tracking adapts by size automatically; mockups may need the tracking values below. ## Using custom fonts Check custom faces against platform size recommendations and actual conditions. Implement Dynamic Type and Bold Text behavior equivalent to the system faces. Apple’s Unity accessibility plug-in can support Dynamic Type in games; if unsuitable, offer a separate text-size adjustment. ## Supporting Dynamic Type Dynamic Type is available in iOS, iPadOS, tvOS, visionOS, and watchOS. Test every supported size, including Larger Accessibility Text on iPhone/iPad. Scale meaningful glyphs as well as text; SF Symbols integrate automatically. Preserve useful information at the largest accessibility size rather than aggressively truncating. Give labels enough lines and avoid truncation in scrolling regions unless a detail view exposes the full text. Stack inline timestamps/glyphs beneath or above primary text, grow containers, and reduce columns when width becomes cramped. Original implementation guidance derived from the source. A scroll view reveals content beyond its bounds through vertical or horizontal movement. The container is visually neutral; transient indicators communicate position and scrolling, with platform-specific behavior. ## Best practices Keep system gestures, keyboard shortcuts, and elastic feedback. Suggest offscreen content with partial items at edges because indicators are not always visible. Avoid nested scrolling on the same axis; orthogonal nested scrolling is acceptable. Page-by-page movement can suit fixed chunks; retain a small overlap, such as a line or part of an image, to preserve context. Automatically reveal hidden relevant content when locating a search result, typing at an offscreen insertion point, extending selection beyond an edge, or acting on a selection after scrolling away. Move only as far as needed; a partially visible selection need not be fully recentered. Bound zoom to useful minimum and maximum scales. ## Scroll edge effects In iOS, iPadOS, and macOS, edge effects separate floating UI from scrolling content beneath. Prefer automatic styling; it provides stronger separation for dense toolbars, uncontained text, or pinned headers. Thoroughly test legibility if choosing soft styling. The hard style gives a more defined opaque boundary; the soft style fades through a variable blur. Use an effect only where floating controls overlap a scroll view, not as decoration or a dark overlay. Apply one per view; split panes can each have one, with aligned heights. ## Platform considerations ### iOS, iPadOS A page control can show position in paged scrolling. Suppress the scroll indicator on that same axis to avoid redundant signals. ### macOS Scroll indicators are also called scroll bars. Small or mini bars can suit tight panels; match other control sizes in that panel. ### tvOS Scrolling follows focus automatically to keep focused content visible, without distinct scroll-view objects and indicators. ### visionOS A small fixed-size indicator stays at the vertical center of the trailing edge or horizontal center of the bottom edge. Swiping reveals it; looking and dragging it enables a jog bar that adjusts scrolling speed rather than absolute position, with tick marks communicating acceleration. Allow adequate margin because this indicator is slightly thicker than on iOS. #### Look to Scroll Eye-only scrolling starts near a scroll boundary and coexists with gestures. Opt in separately for each reading or browsing scroll view; the behavior is not automatic. Avoid it for secondary controls or dense views needing precise quick movement. Apply it consistently across comparable content. Full-width or full-height regions give generous, understandable boundaries; inset regions need clear edges. Remove custom scroll-position effects such as parallax or animation before enabling it to prevent unpredictable behavior. ### watchOS Prefer vertical content that works with the Digital Crown. Use vertical tab views for page-based navigation, with an indicator beside the crown. Keep pages near one screen tall when possible; long pages can scroll and the page indicator expands into a scroll indicator. Use variable heights sparingly and preferably after short fixed pages. ## Resources Official implementation links and revision metadata follow. #### Related [Page controls](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/page-controls) [Gestures](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/gestures) [Pointing devices](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/pointing-devices) #### Developer documentation — SwiftUI — UIKit — AppKit — WatchKit — SwiftUI ## Change log Revision dates recorded by Apple: June 8, 2026, March 24, 2026, July 28, 2025, February 2, 2024, December 5, 2023, June 5, 2023.

# Separate image presentation from action

Read [the image-view guide](../../references/image-views.md). Use the following as application advice, preserving the requested stack.

Inspect the image assets and container, target platform, intended focal content, and whether the request is to create, review, or adapt. Determine whether the image is decorative, informative, editable, or an action. Record intrinsic resolution/aspect ratio, crop/fit behavior, overlays, and animation source when available; a screenshot cannot establish frame preparation or input semantics.

Choose fitting from the content's purpose: preserve the whole image when cropping loses information; allow deliberate cropping when the focal subject survives. Do not stretch photographs to satisfy a container. If activation performs an action, use button semantics rather than attaching an unexplained gesture to a display image. On Mac, choose an image well for copy/paste/drag/Delete editing. Prefer symbols or template imagery for interface glyphs rather than embedding their appearance as arbitrary pictures.

# Operate on buttons

Read [the buttons guide](../../references/buttons.md) before making HIG claims. This procedure is application advice for turning that guide into an artifact; platform facts and dimensions come from the guide. Preserve the user's framework and authorized scope.

## Establish the action contract

Inspect the supplied screen, code, prototype, or brief. Identify the target platform, input methods, surrounding task, and requested mode: create, review, or adapt. For each consequential button, record its visible label or symbol, activation outcome, affected object, reversibility, current role/default status, and actual hit region if available. A screenshot can establish visible styling; it cannot establish hit geometry, keyboard behavior, or accessible names. Mark those as unknown and inspect implementation when available.

Classify the action before styling it. An immediate command fits a button. A persistent on/off setting may need a toggle; choosing one of several persistent options may need a segmented control or picker; a menu-opening control needs the corresponding menu button behavior. Retain a button when its action is to open that choice, but distinguish opening from committing a choice.

## Make and apply the consequential choices

1. Write an outcome-specific short verb phrase, or use a familiar symbol whose meaning survives its context. Give an icon-only control an accessible name that states the action. Do not assume a tooltip replaces the name. On Mac, an ellipsis indicates that another window, view, or app requires further input; add it based on the continuation, not merely because an operation takes time.
2. Assign semantic roles from consequences. Prefer one or two prominent likely actions per view and use style rather than unequal sizes to rank related choices. A primary/default action should normally be the likely nondestructive choice. If destruction is involved, consult the alerts topic before deciding confirmation and Return behavior: the guide explicitly allows a deliberate-destruction alert exception, so “destructive can never be default” is not a universal rule. Cancel abandons the current task; it is not a generic label for completing it.
3. Choose the system control/style when available, retaining its states and accessibility behavior. For a custom control, specify perceivable press feedback and preserve meaningful focus, enabled/disabled, and selected states as applicable. State the reason for a disabled action when the surrounding context does not explain it. This is application advice, not a new Apple requirement to add all states to every button.
4. Check visual and selectable geometry separately. Apply the guide's target and separation rules for the actual platform; a small glyph or small visual style does not establish a small hit region. On visionOS, retain a discernible shape/fill, use standard audible/state feedback, and inspect center spacing and hover overlap. Do not propose unsupported custom hover effects or haptics there. On watchOS, choose inline versus toolbar placement deliberately; preserve common heights for peer controls and use short labels for side-by-side actions. On Mac, distinguish view-body square/image/help buttons from toolbar items; apply the help-button placement/count rules only when designing Help.

On iOS/iPadOS, use the activating button's activity indication as described in the guide, preserving context and replacing its image when appropriate. Perform the authorized work: implement the controls in the supplied project for a build request; produce an annotated control specification for a design request; or report evidence-backed defects and exact corrections for a review. Return the changed artifact or a compact button contract containing label/name, outcome, role/default, style/placement, target region, and relevant state behavior. In review mode attach findings to identifiable controls and separate observed defects from checks requiring execution.

Verify that activation reaches the named outcome; cancellation leaves the intended prior state; keyboard/default activation cannot commit an unintended outcome; focus and accessible names identify the action; and enlarged labels do not clip or overlap adjacent targets. Measure hit regions from layout/runtime data when available. ## Worked transformation

**Before:** A Mac photo organizer has equally prominent `Go`, `Remove`, and `Close` buttons. `Go` opens export settings; `Remove` deletes a selection with undo; `Close` finishes editing metadata.

**Decision:** The labels hide three different contracts. Export requires further input; routine reversible removal does not by itself justify a confirmation alert; finishing edits should name completion. The export task, rather than removal, is the likely action on this screen.

# Adaptive photo album — iOS and iPadOS

## Scope and task

Browse, identify, open, and select photos in albums containing 0, 20, or 20,000 items. Preserve the existing product and implementation framework; no framework is supplied. A collection remains appropriate because visual recognition is the primary task. The following geometry, thresholds, loading budgets, and navigation choices are product decisions, not Apple-prescribed measurements.

## Layout contract

Use one vertical scrolling collection inside the current window's safe area. Header contains album title, localized item count, and Select. Keep controls outside photographs. Respect system navigation and Back gestures. Do not nest a second vertical scroller around the grid. Show the native scroll indicator and allow partial rows to suggest more content.

Let W be safe-area width in points. Use 16 pt leading/trailing margins and 8 pt horizontal/vertical cell gaps. Available grid width A = W − 32. At ordinary text sizes, minimum cell width M = 104 pt. Column count C = max(1, floor((A + 8)/(M + 8))); cell width S = (A − 8(C − 1))/C. Never add columns based on item count or stretch an incomplete last row. For supported widths smaller than M + 32, use one cell fitted to A. All interactive targets remain at least 44 × 44 pt, with separate nonoverlapping hit regions.

| Safe-area W | Columns | Cell width S |
|---|---:|---:|
| 320 pt | 2 | 140 pt |
| 390 pt | 3 | 114 pt |
| 768 pt | 6 | 116 pt |
| 1024 pt | 8 | 117 pt |

These are width examples, not device breakpoints: a narrow iPad window follows the narrow rule. Resize continuously on rotation, multitasking, or Display Zoom without changing album, order, selection, or open photo. Keep focus rings inside each cell's reserved space without covering neighboring content.

Use semantic system title, body, and caption styles with Dynamic Type and Bold Text. Each cell has an image and a caption below it on a semantic background: user title if available, otherwise localized capture date/time, otherwise filename. Caption may use two lines at ordinary sizes; full text is always available in photo detail. At accessibility text sizes use M = 240 pt, growing caption height with unlimited lines and stacking metadata. Reduce columns further if measured text cannot fit; never shrink text to retain density. Header controls wrap into additional rows rather than clipping. Preserve all actions through at least 200% text enlargement and the largest supported accessibility size.

## Image meaning and detail

Fit the entire photo proportionally in a square image area using neutral letterboxing; never stretch it. This conservative choice avoids hiding subjects when focal-point metadata is absent. Use an image inside a system button, with a single accessible element grouping image and caption. In browse mode activation opens that photo's detail. Detail shows the whole photo and complete caption, known description, date, and filename, and offers Back. Back restores the originating photo and scroll context.

Accessible name: title plus a known content description when it adds information, then date/time; fallback to filename and “Description unavailable.” Do not invent a visual description from a filename or present metadata as a full equivalent of photo content. Expose button role and selected state separately; do not repeat the caption as a second focus stop. Example with supplied metadata: “Maya at the beach, sunset behind Maya, October 12, 2026, 18:03.” The dataset must supply useful descriptions for meaningful visual content; missing descriptions remain a content-accessibility limitation.

## Identity, selection, and changes

Maintain immutable photo IDs, an ordered ID snapshot, selected-ID set, mode, open-photo ID, and scroll anchor (first visible photo ID plus its offset from the viewport top). Do not store selection or restoration solely by cell index. Select enters selection mode with an empty set; tapping a cell toggles its membership instead of opening detail. Show a checkmark and outline as well as selected semantics, and a persistent “N selected” count. Done leaves selection mode and explicitly clears selection. Select is unavailable for an empty album. Selection provides state only; downstream batch commands are outside this brief.

Rotation, resizing, background/resume, and return from detail preserve mode and selected IDs. Before reflow capture the anchor; after reflow restore its row to the same viewport offset, clamped at the ends. Preserve accessibility/keyboard focus on its photo ID and reveal only as far as necessary. Explicit Done or leaving the album ends selection. Persist album route, open photo, selection, and anchor for restoration where the implementation supports scene restoration; specify and test this before claiming process-relaunch restoration.

Defer background insertions/reordering while scrolling or selecting; show an “Update Album” button when a new snapshot is ready. Activation applies it while retaining surviving selected IDs and anchor. If an item is removed externally, remove its ID from selection, update the count with an accessible notification, and use the next surviving item in the old order as anchor/focus, otherwise the previous item. If none survives, enter empty state. Never substitute a new photo at the old numeric index. User reordering and deletion commands are not introduced.

## Scale and retrieval

Use the same layout and identity rules for 20 and 20,000 photos. For 20, all metadata may load together; show the incomplete final row naturally. For 20,000, virtualize/reuse cells and page ordered metadata in batches of 200 with stable cursors over the album snapshot. Fetch a lightweight month-to-first-ID index and total count independently, so reaching older photos does not require downloading preceding thumbnails.

For albums over 200 items, show a labeled “Jump to Month” button opening a dedicated month index screen with year headings, month buttons, counts, and Back. Activating a month loads its metadata page and reveals its first photo, retaining selection; cancellation returns to the unchanged anchor. Unknown capture dates form a final “Date Unknown” group. Keep order chronological newest first, with immutable ID tie-breaks; no ranking-driven reshuffles. For small albums omit this navigation. This threshold is a product choice.

Decode thumbnails off the main thread at rendered pixel size; prioritize visible cells and prefetch at most one viewport before/after. Cancel stale requests on reuse and verify returned photo ID and rendition size before display. Cap decoded thumbnail cache at 64 MiB with eviction; lower it under memory pressure. Fetch full-resolution content only for the open detail and release it on exit. Metadata pagination must not rebuild or decode the entire album. These budgets require profiling, and are not verified performance claims.

## States and controls

- Initial loading: retain title and Back; show “Loading photos…” until metadata resolves. Do not display empty copy during loading.
- Ready: show actual count and cells. Thumbnail loading reserves image/caption geometry; failure shows “Preview unavailable” and a labeled Retry Preview action in detail. Keep metadata and selection usable.
- Empty, only after successful zero count: “No Photos in This Album” and “Photos added to this album will appear here.” Keep Back available; do not invent an import capability.
- Metadata failure: “Couldn’t Load Photos” with Retry; retain already loaded cells, selection, and anchor. Further-page failure appears after the loaded content with Retry, never as a false end of album. Retry repeats only the failed request and suppresses duplicates while pending.
- Month jump failure: retain the index and offer Retry without resetting the grid's saved context.

Use system buttons with short visible labels, standard press/focus feedback, and minimum 44 × 44 pt targets. Back, Select, Done, Update Album, Jump to Month, month choices, and Retry have their stated immediate outcomes and ordinary nondestructive roles. Keep Retry context visible while its activity indication runs. Every operation is available by touch, keyboard/Full Keyboard Access, and assistive activation; pointer hover is optional feedback. Arrow navigation follows displayed rows, activation opens/toggles as appropriate, and standard system shortcuts remain intact. Scrolling must never activate a photo.

Expose album title and month/year headings for assistive navigation. Reading order follows locale order across each row then downward; captions stay with photos. Loading changes must not steal focus or announce every thumbnail. Announce relevant errors, selected-count changes, and snapshot updates. Use semantic foreground/background colors; selection must remain understandable without color. Measure contrast in light/dark and Increase Contrast. With Reduce Motion use immediate reflow and state changes without zoom/spring transitions; preserve identity and location.

## Source basis

Local installed HIG snapshot consulted; official links identify guidance, not a live web verification:

- [Collections — Best practices and iOS/iPadOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/collections): familiar grids, selectable items, understandable layout changes; explicit updates preferred during interaction.
- [Layout — Adaptability and safe areas](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/layout), [iOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ios), [iPadOS](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/designing-for-ipados): adapt to available space and preserve task context.
- [Typography — Supporting Dynamic Type](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/typography), [Accessibility](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/accessibility), [VoiceOver — Descriptions and Navigation](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/voiceover): reflow, meaningful equivalents, semantics, input access, and preferences.
- [Image views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/image-views), [Buttons](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/buttons), [Scroll views](https://developer.apple.com/design/human-interface-guidelines/scroll-views): actionable image semantics, standard controls, one scroll owner, and minimal reveal.

Acceptance matrix and evidence status are recorded in result.md.
